name: Tomas Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group without ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign, and this interview is confidential. You can separate a public answer from what you privately think. What happens in a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Tomas, 43, and I'm a junior electrician with a vocational certificate. I work under supervision wiring homes and repairing small businesses, and I'm still less skilled and slower than most of the crew. Today I prepared cable routes in a row of flats and had to ask twice which drawing matched the room. I like seeing the pieces fit, but I get tired of being the person who needs another check.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your situation outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works part time at a community sports centre, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My pay is typical for the trade, but this contract ends in nine months; we have two months of expenses saved and some other electrical employers nearby. I use an AI note tool occasionally after a senior colleague has tried it first, never instead of asking for a practical check. I think paid adult learning should be a shared responsibility, with workers able to ask together rather than each taking the risk alone.

say: I'd welcome **fewer announcements** and time to finish the flats properly while the office saved copying time.
I'd still ask whether **paid work** would continue after the present contract ended.
think: The **nine-month contract end** would still worry me even if AI stayed a small part of the job.
Two months of **expenses saved** helps a search, without paying the mortgage indefinitely between jobs.
do: Ask now for the next **contract decision date** and watch posted junior electrical vacancies nearby.
Apply for **posted supervised roles** if renewal remains unconfirmed three months before expiry, checking written wages, hours and affordable travel.
feel: **Anxious** about finding the next job, with a reserve and a vacancy search giving some room to act.
S0.quote: A quiet technology story wouldn't renew my contract.
fieldNote: His **baseline anxiety** follows an existing fixed end date, not an assumption that minor AI savings automatically remove practical work.
He distinguishes **reassuring words** from a renewed contract and restricts applications to supervised work within his actual junior competence.

steps.text: Apply for supervised junior jobs if renewal is unconfirmed three months before expiry
Check posted vacancies for written wages, hours and affordable travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew I'd welcome fewer announcements and more time to finish the flats properly. If the office saved time on copying, good. I'd still want to know whether there was paid work when this contract ended.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be anxious even if AI stayed small, because the nine-month end date would still be on my contract. Two months of expenses helps, but the mortgage doesn't wait while I search. A quiet technology story wouldn't renew my contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the supervisor when the next paid project and contract decision would be known. I'd start watching actual posted junior electrical vacancies nearby rather than wait for the last month. In the first plateau year I'd apply for suitable supervised roles with written wages and hours if renewal wasn't confirmed three months before the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the next job rather than frightened of a machine. I can look around and we have a little reserve, so I don't feel stuck. I'd still check the calendar more often than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the supervisor said there would probably be more work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the decision date in writing and keep my own application date three months before the contract ended. A friendly remark in the van isn't a new contract. I could appreciate the reassurance without spending it on the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of vacancy would you apply for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for junior duties with supervision and check the wage after travel. I wouldn't apply as an experienced independent electrician because the salary looked nicer. A vocational certificate isn't the same as experience I haven't gained.

say: I'd ask **faster planning** to leave time for teaching the junior who still does the practical work.
I'd back a **shared paid-practice request** while using proven tools with real instruction and checks.
think: The **contract end** still worries me, while tighter schedules could make the next junior job harder to find.
I don't expect software to fit cable immediately, but I still need **supervision** to earn safely elsewhere.
do: Join the **workers' association** and request named paid practice without reduced wages.
Try the proven **note assistant** only during paid time with supervisor checks, while retaining the job-application deadline.
feel: **Anxious** about the next contract, alongside cautious curiosity about an already checked tool.
S1.quote: An unpaid place could be well meant and still wrong for our mortgage.
fieldNote: He sees **task compression** as a possible pressure on a future junior vacancy, rather than immediate replacement of hands-on electrical fitting.
His **learning request** protects wages as well as fees, while occasional tool use depends on prior checking and paid instruction.

steps.text: Join the workers association and request named paid practice without wage reduction
Try the proven note assistant only in paid time with supervisor checks
Apply for supervised junior jobs if renewal is unconfirmed before the deadline
Check posted vacancies for written wages, hours and affordable travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster planning should include time to teach the person doing the work. I'd back the crew asking together for paid practice instead of every junior buying a course in secret. We could use a proven tool without pretending it removed the need for a teacher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be worried about the contract end, and about whether the next project needed as many juniors if schedules were tighter. Most of my work is practical, so I don't expect software to fit the cable tomorrow. But I could face a harder search while still needing supervision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd join the local workers' association and support a request for named paid practice with no wage reduction. In the first year I'd try the firm's proven note assistant only during paid time, with my supervisor checking the record. I'd keep the same application deadline if a renewed contract wasn't confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the next contract, with curiosity about a tool somebody had already checked. I wouldn't feel panicked. I would want learning time to be paid time rather than another bill or lost evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you ask the association to seek?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for one weekly session with a named experienced worker on tasks within my training. I'd want the wage protected as well as any course fee. An unpaid place could be well meant and still wrong for our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm wanted immediate use of an unfamiliar tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask them to show me what had been checked and what paid instruction came with it. I wouldn't send an unchecked note because I was afraid of looking difficult. I'd keep asking through the association if it became a repeated pressure.

say: I'd separate **2028 thinking work** from robots around 2031 without treating the gap as a renewed contract.
I'd ask for **paid junior routes** before competition narrows the chances to gain practical experience.
think: I could lose **hours or another contract** as firms prepare for capable hands-on robots.
Two months of **savings** gives only a short careful search while my limited skill narrows the available roles.
do: Compare actual **funded places** and posted junior vacancies with help from the association now.
Enroll in practical **training** before 2028 only with covered fees and maintained paid hours.
Apply after 2028 for workable **supervised maintenance jobs** and check lender or support options if income falls.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic income loss, while uncertain about its extent and able to use a plan.
S2.quote: The three-year robot gap isn't a promise about my next contract.
fieldNote: He states **real income risk** without claiming that catastrophic loss is certain, supporting anxiety rather than an automatic higher mood.
He keeps **support and training** conditional and checks supervision, travel and written wages before treating any vacancy as a usable offer.

steps.text: Enroll in practical training only with covered fees and maintained paid hours
Apply after 2028 for posted supervised maintenance jobs with workable written wages after travel
Check actual lender options and support eligibility if income falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that thinking work changes in 2028, with hands-on robots following around 2031. The three-year robot gap isn't a promise about my next contract. I'd want paid routes for juniors before we were competing for fewer chances to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose hours or fail to find another junior contract as firms prepared for the robot stage. Two months of expenses would let us search carefully for a short while, not wait years for something suitable. I'd be worried about losing income while still too inexperienced for better roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd use the association to compare actual funded training places and posted junior vacancies. I'd enroll before 2028 only if fees were covered and my paid hours maintained. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for supervised maintenance roles with written wages that worked after travel, and ask the lender about actual options if income fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, more sharply than in the plateau, but not convinced a total wage loss was certain. I could ask for help, keep applying and use the reserve carefully. The hard part would be not treating the first offer as the only possible one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the mortgage if income fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the end date and household bills on paper with my partner before the search became urgent. If income fell, we'd ask what the lender could offer and check support eligibility, not assume either was approved. I wouldn't tell the children the house was safe on the strength of a form we'd only just sent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could make you turn down a vacancy even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether the duties were supervised and whether the hours and wage were written down. If the travel made the pay unworkable, I'd keep looking rather than call the job a rescue. I couldn't safely sell practical experience I didn't have.

say: I'd use **five years** to make paid training normal, asking now rather than waiting for 2031.
I'd keep the **2034 robot stage** visible as the same hands-on change arriving later.
think: More time could improve my **practical competence** before the hardest changes to electrical work.
The current **nine-month contract end** still threatens income unless renewal or another paid job is confirmed.
do: Keep the **application deadline** and support the association request for paid supervised practice.
Take practical **training** before 2031 only with covered fees and protected paid hours.
Apply after 2031 for posted **supervised roles** matching completed skills and improving written pay after travel.
feel: **Anxious** about the present contract, with less technology pressure and no assumed increase in savings.
S3.quote: A later robot date doesn't sign the next contract for me.
fieldNote: He preserves **baseline contract anxiety** under a longer timeline instead of confusing preparation time with current job renewal.
His **training test** connects checked competence with actual advertised work, and a delayed decision still triggers applications before expiry.

steps.text: Support the association request for paid supervised practice
Take practical training only with covered fees and protected paid hours
Apply for posted supervised jobs matching completed skills and better pay after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years should let us turn paid training into a normal part of the job. I'd still ask for it now, with the crew, not wait until 2031. Robots around 2034 would still be the same hands-on change later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I'd have more time to become useful before the hardest change. But this contract would still end in nine months unless it was renewed. A later robot date doesn't sign the next contract for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the application deadline and the association's paid-practice request. I'd take practical training before 2031 only with covered fees and paid hours protected. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply for posted supervised roles with better written pay after travel, based on whatever skills I'd actually completed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the current contract, with less pressure from the technology date. I'd welcome more time to learn. I wouldn't pretend the two-month reserve had grown just because the timeline did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would show that training was improving your earning options?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at tasks I could now do correctly under the required checks and whether employers actually advertised that work. A course title wouldn't be enough by itself. I want learning that reaches a paid job, not just another folder at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the contract decision kept being delayed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd start the applications at the deadline I'd set. I'd keep working and ask for written reference details while the supervisor could still see my work. Leaving early without another wage wouldn't help the household.

say: I'd ask for **paid learning** now while using the decade to check what actually happens each year.
I wouldn't let a **promise for 2036** replace teaching needed for next week's electrical work.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I would still need earnings without assuming future retirement income or lower household costs.
The **next contract gap** remains my immediate worry, regardless of a more distant technology date.
do: Keep the **application deadline** and support the association request for named paid practice.
Take practical **training** before 2036 only with funded fees and maintained paid hours.
Apply after 2036 for posted **repair roles** matching completed skills and offering workable written wages after travel.
feel: **Anxious** about near-term income, with more hope about learning and no assumptions about future household support.
S4.quote: A promise for 2036 wouldn't teach me next week's job.
fieldNote: He separates **preparation time** from the fixed contract decision that already shapes the household's next year.
His **annual progress check** requires actual correctly performed tasks and paid work, while future children's income and retirement remain uncounted.

steps.text: Support the association request for named paid supervised practice
Take practical training only with funded fees and maintained paid hours
Apply for posted repair jobs matching completed skills and workable wages after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives the employer time to plan paid learning properly, and gives workers time to ask together for it. I'd still keep checking what actually happened each year. A promise for 2036 wouldn't teach me next week's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 when full thinking AI arrived and around 56 when robots followed, still needing earnings unless our actual finances changed. But my first question would remain the contract ending in nine months. I can't jump over the next wage gap because the big technology date is further away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep the same application deadline and ask the association to keep named paid practice on its agenda. I'd take practical training before 2036 only with funded fees and maintained paid hours. In the first year after 2036 I'd apply for posted repair roles matching my completed skills, checking written wages and travel before any change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the next contract, but more hopeful about having time to become good at the work. I wouldn't assume the children being older or being in my fifties solved the household budget. I would want the next year to improve, not just the distant plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge progress over the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write down each new task I could do correctly with the required supervision and whether it helped me find paid work. If the list didn't grow, I'd question the arrangement with the association. I wouldn't call ten years in the trade ten years of learning if nobody had taught me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change plans for the children because of the longer timeline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn't choose their studies from this picture or rely on them to replace our wages. I'd tell them that asking for paid help while learning is reasonable. I want them to see a plan with real work in it, not an adult pretending not to worry.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because an already uncertain next contract could become a much harder search while I'm still junior. Paid practical places with covered fees and a clear decision date for work would help. My mortgage needs the next wage, not a confident speech about the next decade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the person has a permanent job before telling them how many years they have to prepare. A technology timeline and a contract timeline can run beside each other without matching. I need to plan for both.

headlineQuote: My mortgage needs the next wage, not a confident speech about the next decade.
portrait: **Tomas, 43**, is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, typical trade pay and a contract ending in nine months.
He and **his partner** have two school-age children, a mortgage, two months of expenses saved and some similar employers nearby.
He uses **proven AI occasionally**, keeps practical work supervised and favours collective requests for paid teaching with maintained wages.
Every scenario retains **contract anxiety**; faster change could narrow the next job search, while longer timelines improve learning prospects without renewing work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could make an already uncertain contract search harder before he gains stronger practical skills.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practical places** with covered fees would make learning achievable.
A clear **work decision date** would help him plan the household's next wage.
